claims.text: Compositional complexity can be represented by the degree of atomic-size mismatch and chemical heterogeneity.
Compositional complexity governs premelting behavior in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Atomic-size mismatch and chemical heterogeneity create localized lattice distortions.
Atomic-size mismatch and chemical heterogeneity create heterogeneous surface-energy distributions.
Localized lattice distortions and heterogeneous surface energies lower the energy barrier for surface disordering before bulk melting.
Nanoparticle size and support conditions can be held constant while alloy composition and atomic-size mismatch are varied.
Supported high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can be prepared with controlled size and stability.
Greater compositional complexity increases variability in interatomic bonding at nanoparticle surfaces.
Greater bond variability produces weaker and more heterogeneous surface bonding.
Weaker and more heterogeneous surface bonding promotes surface premelting at temperatures below the full melting point.
The nanoparticle core remains stabilized by high-entropy features while the surface premelts.
Nanoparticles with greater atomic-size mismatch will have an earlier premelting onset than lower-mismatch baseline nanoparticles.
The full melting temperature of the core will shift less than the premelting-onset temperature.
The proposed relationship should hold for nanoparticles smaller than approximately 100 nm.
The proposed relationship requires compositions in which mixing alters surface-energy distributions without introducing secondary phases.
Nanoparticle-support interactions and particle morphology may affect the quantitative shift in premelting onset.
A distinct DSC heat-capacity change can identify premelting onset.
Failure to observe a statistically significant premelting-onset difference between size- and support-matched high- and low-mismatch series would falsify the hypothesis.
